key_points: BTPNA creates a planned transparenchymal tunnel from an airway point-of-entry (POE) to a peripheral pulmonary nodule.
High diagnostic yield (≈73–75 %) including nodules without a bronchus sign.
Lower pneumothorax risk than TTNA by using an avascular, airway-based pathway.
Requires advanced navigation (Archimedes VBN) and fused fluoroscopy under general anesthesia.
Working channel requirements: ≥2.0 mm for Fle XNeedle+balloon; ≥2.8 mm when using a sheath.

clinical_procedures.name: BTPNA Planning
steps: Obtain high-resolution chest CT and reconstruct 3D model with navigation software (e.g., Archimedes).
Identify an optimal POE on the airway wall and an avascular path to the nodule.
Confirm feasibility relative to nearby critical structures on CT (vessels, heart, esophagus).
notes: General anesthesia and muscle paralysis planned for the procedure.

clinical_procedures.name: Navigation and pathway setup
steps: Insert bronchoscope and navigate to the predetermined POE under navigation guidance.
Puncture the airway wall with a coring needle or Fle XNeedle to create the initial opening.
Dilate the puncture with a balloon catheter to establish a tunnel entrance.
Advance a sheath with a blunt dissection stylet through lung parenchyma to the lesion under real-time fluoroscopy/navigation.
notes: Fused fluoroscopy overlays the planned pathway onto live fluoroscopy to ensure on-course advancement.

clinical_procedures.name: Sampling through sheath
steps: Remove the blunt stylet and use forceps, brush, and/or needle aspiration through the sheath to obtain tissue.
Employ multiple sampling tools to maximize representativeness.
notes: Confirm sheath position at the lesion under fused fluoroscopy before sampling.

clinical_procedures.name: Postprocedure monitoring and complication management
steps: Monitor for pneumothorax; obtain chest imaging if symptomatic and manage with observation or chest tube as indicated.
Manage hemorrhage with local measures; escalate to vascular/surgical intervention if major vessel injury occurs.
Use aseptic technique; consider antibiotics per local protocol to prevent infection; monitor for bronchial injury.

clinical_procedures.name: Equipment compatibility
steps: Working channel ≥2.0 mm when using only Fle XNeedle and balloon catheter.
Working channel ≥2.8 mm when using a sheath with Fle XNeedle and balloon catheter.
notes: Select instruments compatible with bronchoscope channel to avoid obstruction.

diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Enhances diagnostic yield while minimizing complications such as pneumothorax compared to TTNA.
limitations: technical challenges for certain lesion locations.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Particularly for nodules without a bronchus sign or not directly accessible via traditional bronchoscopy.

treatment_algorithms.title: BTPNA surgical procedure algorithm (planning, pathway setup, sampling)
treatment_algorithms.condition: Peripheral pulmonary nodules (PPNs) targeted with BTPNA
specific_recommendations: Initially, high-resolution CT scans of the patient’s chest are obtained.
The CT data are then processed using advanced navigation software ... which reconstructs the imaging into a comprehensive three-dimensional model.
The software’s ability to identify an avascular path from the POE to the nodule is crucial.
The patient is placed under general anesthesia to ensure comfort and immobility during the procedure.
A coring needle is then used to puncture the airway wall, creating the initial opening for the tunnel.
This opening is enlarged by the insertion of a balloon catheter, which is inflated to dilate the puncture site.
A sheath equipped with a blunt dissection stylet is carefully advanced through the lung parenchyma, using real-time guidance from fluoroscopy or the navigation system.
Through this sheath, various biopsy tools, such as forceps and brushes, are introduced to collect tissue samples from the nodule.
decision_points_and_pathways: (a) Puncture at the POE guided by navigation
(b) Balloon catheter used to dilate the tunnel
(d) Confirmation of sheath position at the lesion under fused fluoroscopy
(e) Biopsy of the lesion under fused fluoroscopy guidance

monitoring_requirements: Using real-time guidance from fluoroscopy or the navigation system

clinical_guidelines.title: Indications: Peripheral Pulmonary Nodule Biopsy
specific_recommendations: The primary clinical application of BTPNA lies in the diagnosis of PPNs

integration of BTPNA with the Archimedes navigation system has yielded remarkable results, providing a high diagnostic yield ranging from 72.8 % to 75.4 %, regardless of the presence of a bronchus sign
BTPNA has shown even greater efficacy for lesions without a bronchus sign that are not directly accessible via traditional bronchoscopy, achieving diagnostic yields between 71.4 % and 74.1 %

When compared to other bronchoscopic techniques, such as transbronchial needle aspiration and transbronchial biopsy, which have diagnostic yields of 59.1 % and 22.6 %, respectively, BTPNA has proven to be superior. It boasts a biopsy yield of 86.3 %, significantly outperforming guided TBNA, which only achieved a 67.2 % yield
In contrast to TTNA, which has a substantial pneumothorax risk of up to 15 %, BTPNA’s bronchoscopic approach significantly reduces this risk

outcome_measures: diagnostic yields between 71.4 % and 74.1 % for lesions without a bronchus sign
guided TBNA 67.2 % vs BTPNA biopsy yield 86.3 %
TTNA pneumothorax risk of up to 15 %
alternative_approaches: transbronchial needle aspiration and transbronchial biopsy

clinical_guidelines.title: Contraindications for BTPNA
specific_recommendations: patients who are not suitable candidates for routine bronchoscopy or general anesthesia
Patients with severe cardiovascular disease, advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or other significant comorbidities
patients with a bleeding tendency whether due to coagulopathy, use of anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications, or thrombocytopenia
Vascular wrapping, where the nodule or the pathway is encircled by significant blood vessels
proximity to critical structures such as the heart, major arteries, or the esophagus
Patients with advanced pulmonary conditions, such as severe emphysema, bullae, mediastinal emphysema, or a history of pneumothorax
Lesions located at the apex of the lung are particularly problematic due to the steep angles required to reach these areas
lesions that are surrounded by blood vessels or located in regions where there is a significant angle between the bronchial tract and the lesion

clinical_guidelines.title: Complications management in BTPNA
clinical_guidelines.condition: BTPNA-related complications (pneumothorax, hemorrhage, infection, bronchial injury)
specific_recommendations: Minor cases of pneumothorax are often managed conservatively, with close monitoring through chest X-rays.
In more severe cases of pneumothorax, the insertion of a chest tube may be required to evacuate the air and reexpand the lung.
Minor bleeding can often be controlled with local pressure or the application of hemostatic agents.
If a major blood vessel is inadvertently injured, it may lead to severe hemorrhage, requiring more aggressive interventions, such as vascular intervention or even surgical repair.
Adhering to strict aseptic techniques during the procedure.
Use of broad-spectrum antibiotics before and after the procedure can help prevent or treat infections.
Bronchial injury prevention: precise procedural techniques, including careful navigation and controlled advancement of instruments.
Bronchial injury management: conservative observation or surgical intervention if more severe.
decision_points_and_pathways: Pneumothorax: minor (monitor with chest X-rays) vs severe (insert chest tube).
Hemorrhage: minor (local pressure/hemostatic agents) vs major vessel injury (vascular intervention or surgical repair).
Bronchial injury: minor (close observation) vs more severe (surgical intervention).
monitoring_requirements: Close monitoring through chest X-rays for minor pneumothorax
Careful postprocedural monitoring for signs of infection

Selection of appropriate tools, such as the Fle XNeedle for precise airway puncture and balloon catheters for safe dilation.
Continuous real-time monitoring during the procedure, using fluoroscopy and navigation systems.

technology_and_technique.topic: BTPNA diagnostic role for peripheral pulmonary nodules (PPNs)
technology_and_technique.summary: BTPNA enables creation of a direct, planned transparenchymal tunnel from an airway point-of-entry to a target nodule, overcoming limitations of conventional bronchoscopy that requires a bronchus sign. The chapter notes high diagnostic yield, particularly for nodules lacking a bronchus sign, while minimizing complications compared with transthoracic needle aspiration.

technology_and_technique.topic: Technology and navigation (Archimedes Virtual Bronchoscopy Navigation)
technology_and_technique.summary: The Archimedes VBN system integrates CT to build a 3D model of airways, ribs, lungs, and vasculature, selects an optimal airway point-of-entry, and plans an avascular path to the lesion. Real-time fused fluoroscopy guides a catheter-based tool and a blunt dissection stylet/sheath to the target under general anesthesia with muscle paralysis, supporting accurate sampling and reduced complication risk.

technology_and_technique.topic: Comparative effectiveness: BTPNA vs conventional bronchoscopy and TTNA
technology_and_technique.summary: BTPNA addresses anatomical constraints that limit conventional bronchoscopy (dependence on a bronchus leading to the nodule) and reduces pneumothorax risk compared with TTNA by traversing a preplanned avascular parenchymal path from the airway. The chapter emphasizes improved access and safety; specific head-to-head yield or complication percentages are not provided in the excerpt.

Key steps include preprocedural planning on CT to identify an avascular path and airway point-of-entry; use of fused fluoroscopy for real-time guidance; general anesthesia with muscle paralysis to minimize motion; advancement of a sheath with a blunt dissection stylet along the preplanned tunnel for sampling. These steps are highlighted as important to maximize diagnostic success and safety.

technology_and_technique.topic: Tips to improve safety and yield
technology_and_technique.summary: Plan an avascular trajectory on CT-derived 3D models; confirm pathway intraoperatively with fused fluoroscopy; use a blunt dissection stylet to limit vascular injury; maintain general anesthesia and paralysis to enhance targeting accuracy and reduce movement; select a point-of-entry that optimizes a short, straight path to the nodule.

Indications include biopsy of PPNs—especially those without a bronchus sign or lacking a direct bronchial route—lesions in locations where conventional bronchoscopy is limited, and therapeutic procedures such as ablation. The technique is designed to reach nodules irrespective of airway connection by creating a controlled transparenchymal path.

Contraindications include patients unsuitable for routine bronchoscopy and general anesthesia; lesions with vascular encasement or proximity to critical structures on CT; severe emphysema, large bullae, mediastinal emphysema, or existing pneumothorax; and technical challenges related to lesion location that preclude a safe avascular pathway.

Reported complications include pneumothorax, hemorrhage, infection, and bronchial injury. The chapter emphasizes a significantly lower pneumothorax risk compared with TTNA due to an avascular, airway-based approach; exact complication rates are not provided in the excerpt.

BTPNA was first introduced in 2014 by Gerard Silvestri and colleagues as a novel approach enabling transparenchymal access to peripheral nodules. The chapter describes feasibility and application; specific randomized or head-to-head clinical trial outcomes and percentages are not detailed in the excerpt.

points: BTPNA enables a direct, minimally invasive path to PPNs for diagnosis and therapy with a low complication profile.
Integration of navigation and fused fluoroscopy is central to safety and accuracy.
Careful patient selection and planning are essential; broader data will define its role alongside TTNA and guided bronchoscopy.
